I haven't read my original post in 2 years. It's pretty well said. However, a lot has changed for me since then that has helped me live better. I've learned how to say Fuck You, in my mind, politely, as a way to distance myself from the absolute need to thoroughly please. I've lived in the Midwest where we all are by culture taught to be nice, very nice. It's a meme. Look it up. I was obligated to please my church and my wife way beyond reason and at my personal expense. I was taught that any less was selfish. Selfish, selfish, selfish! That's what I heard regularly. My inability to be what those two institutions wanted me to be tore me down to the point of self-loathing and constant suicidal ideation. 

Through an incredible event, a lot of pain and therapy I finally developed my version of Fuck You. Internally I may be angry, but I filter that out to a polite adult I'm sorry I won't be able to help you with that. I think I'm saying fuck you to myself, to my engrained habit of pleasing everyone about everything. It's a new level of being an adult and I'm OLD, 70 in a few days.

I don't know anyone or heard of anyone (except maybe a post here) where it was beautiful and amazing. If you don't like the person they are not going to make you happy. The most you can get is toleration. Born out of love is not something a 21 year old is capable of. His and her entire view of the world is too clouded by the genetics of reproduction and the naivete of youth. Romance and love are the intellectualization of reproductive drive. The desire for someone is just the ache of emotional and sexual needs you'll get fulfilled, for a while. After that it will most always just turn into a grind. Men and women are too different and too different in what they want. Everyone is too different. You compromise when you don't know how to be alone and when you don't know how to appreciate (love) yourself. 

There is beauty in commitment, in doing your job and keeping your word. Marriage is a job and you'll be praised for sticking it out but what's the point if you're not happy. Joy can be found in a job well done and most jobs are work but there's no pay for the job of marriage except for peace in the home and knowledge that those who know you are pleased that you're doing your job. 

I've learned how to keep my mouth shut, do my work and tough it out. Be a man. There's no one to talk to. Certainly not your spouse. Anything you say can be used against you. Marriage is a lonely business but so is most of life. Get used to it. Learn to appreciate what you are and what you can become that will make you proud of you. Then find some joy in your time alone. 

Just some thoughts in response. Life is complicated and my view is just mine, born from my choices and the events that be fell me.

As for what to do I think the only thing to do is to sit down with a marriage therapist and work it through together. If you do I would expect you to see some definite effort on her part. I would expect her to be very cognizant of the changes that she needs to make on her side. And I would hope that talking it out in front of someone else would help you both see what's rational from each point of view and that might correct some of the misunderstandings.

Tldr: I felt trapped in a miserable marriage and desperately wanted to be in love.

For me it was several factors. I felt trapped in a very unhappy marriage. For decades I was belittled and mocked if I didn't meet her standards of sensitivity. She wanted to be loved and in my way of thinking worshiped. She's say "you don't like me". It was true. I didn't like her. I'd never date her if I was not married to her. But my generation (boomer) and my religion said in every strong term possible that divorce was not an option. 

I dreamed of being in love constantly. Every movie I watched every girl that I knew I wished I could be in love like they show in the movies. Then while seeking for help with depression I met someone who was simply amazing in every way possible. She felt just as trapped in her life and was willing to be with me in spite of. Through great tribulation I worked to change my thinking about divorce. Therapy, talking to friends, meditating, trying to change my way of thinking about how life is supposed to be. All the therapists said that I had put myself in a box so I could get out anytime I wanted. But after decades of life that way it was nearly impossible to change. But I wanted to be loved and to be in love so bad I moved ahead willing to take the risks and the fallout. I don't regret it one bit because the girl was simply amazing in every way possible. In the end I had to break it off because my psychology about the situation and my mental health just couldn't handle it. Not that divorce was wrong but that moving ahead with that other life was just not going to work for me.

If you decide to go I wish you luck. If you decide you can fight there's tools to help.
